---
title: "Quiz: stain separation"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Optical density $\mathrm{OD}_c = -\log_{10}(I_c/I_{0,c})$; with the unit stain vectors as the columns of $S$, $\mathbf{od} = S\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf C = S^{-1}\mathbf{od}$.

---

**Q1.** Why can't we unmix brightfield stains directly on the RGB intensities, as we did with fluorescence?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to the transmitted light when a second stain lies on top of the first?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Fluorescence adds light; absorbing stains each transmit a fraction, so two stains **multiply** the transmitted intensity. A product is not a linear mixture. The logarithm (optical density) turns the product into a sum, and the linear model holds in OD.
:::

---

**Q2.** A background pixel has $I = I_0$. What is its optical density, and its stain concentrations?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\log 1 = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\mathrm{OD} = -\log_{10}(1) = 0$ in every channel, so all concentrations are 0. Unstained glass is the origin of the OD space; that is why $I_0$ (the white reference) must be right.
:::

---

**Q3.** Only the direction of a stain vector matters, not its length. Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to $C_k$ if you double the length of column $k$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\mathbf{od} = \sum_k C_k\mathbf s_k$: doubling $\mathbf s_k$ and halving $C_k$ gives the same OD. The concentration is only defined up to that scale, so the vectors are taken as unit vectors and $C_k$ is measured in "OD units along the stain's direction".
:::

---

**Q4.** With H&E only, why add a third column, and what does its concentration map show?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many channels, how many stains? What is perpendicular to both stains?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Three channels and two stains: to invert a $3 \times 3$ matrix we need a third column. The cross product of the two stain vectors is perpendicular to both; its map, the **residual**, is the part of each pixel's OD that the two stains cannot explain. Near zero everywhere means the stain vectors fit; structure in it means wrong vectors, a third stain or pigment.
:::

---

**Q5.** You deconvolve with the published eosin vector, and the hematoxylin map shows a faint copy of the cytoplasm. What is happening, and what would you do?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare with bleed-through in the first unit.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Crosstalk: this slide's eosin differs from the published vector, so part of the eosin OD is attributed to hematoxylin (exactly the bleed-through of a wrong spillover matrix). Estimate the vectors from the image (Macenko), or from single-stained control slides, and check that the residual map drops to noise.
:::

---

**Q6.** Very dark nuclei have $I = 0$ in the red channel. What happens to their optical density, and to the separation?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$-\log_{10}(0)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$-\log_{10}(0)$ is infinite: the pixel must be clipped (for example at $I = 1$, OD $= \log_{10} 255 = 2.41$ for $I_0 = 255$). The true OD may be higher, and one channel is clipped while the others are not, so the pixel's OD direction is wrong: the concentrations of saturated pixels are unreliable. Use a shorter exposure or a brighter lamp.
:::

---

**Q7.** Why is an amount read from the DAB map not a measure of how much protein is present?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How is DAB produced?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
DAB is deposited by an enzyme reaction: the amount depends on incubation time and saturates, and DAB scatters as well as absorbs, so Beer–Lambert holds only roughly. The map is a relative signal: fine for "positive or negative" and for comparisons within one batch, not for absolute amounts.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that the OD of a pixel with two stains is the sum of the ODs each would have alone.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Write $I_c = I_{0,c}\,10^{-s_{c1}C_1}\,10^{-s_{c2}C_2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\mathrm{OD}_c = -\log_{10}(I_c/I_{0,c}) = -\log_{10}(10^{-s_{c1}C_1}) - \log_{10}(10^{-s_{c2}C_2}) = s_{c1}C_1 + s_{c2}C_2$: the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms.
:::
